e d\}\kappa) igr]\ge\max_{c\in M_1\setminus A} igl[-p_{2c}-\mathbf 1\{d'
e c\}\kappa-(-p_{1c}-\mathbf 1\{h_0
e c\}\kappa) igr].\] Under this premise, Pakes et al. Theorem 2.3(a), PDF p. 20, gives the primary joint restriction \(\Pr(Y_1\in A,Y_2\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)\ge\Pr(Y_1\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)^2\). Only when \(\Pr(Y_1\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)>0\) is this equivalent to the ratio form \(\Pr(Y_2\in A\mid Y_1\in A,Y_0=h_0)\ge\Pr(Y_1\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)\); the full-menu case is \(1\ge1\). If \(M_1
e M_2\), entry or exit destroys the single common choice universe required by Condition 2.2: the same inside and outside alternatives must be available in both periods for the samplewise event containment used before Jensen's inequality, whereas entrants or exits create winner--loser comparisons absent at one date. Condition 2.2 and Theorem 2.3(a) therefore cannot be applied directly to the full changing menus. For an arbitrary finite design and response table \(f\), \(f\in F_\kappa\) if and only if \(\kappa\in I_f\), while \(f\in F_\infty\) if and only if \(I_f\) contains \((k_f,+\infty)\) for some finite \(k_f\). Hence every response table feasible at some finite \(\kappa\) is terminal-feasible if and only if, for every \(f\), \(I_f\) is empty or unbounded above; under this response-type condition every rationalizable \(P\) has \(U(P)=+\infty\). In the pure-entry diagnostic \(h_0=a\), \(M_1=\{a,b\}\), \(M_2=\{a,b,c\}\), and \(f_1=b,f_2(a)=a,f_2(b)=b\), period-one choice of \(b\) and period-two choice of \(a\) after \(a\) impose \(p_{2a}-p_{2b}-\kappa<z_a-z_b<p_{1a}-p_{1b}-\kappa\), while period-two persistence in \(b\) imposes \(z_a-z_b<p_{2a}-p_{2b}+\kappa\). Comparisons against the never-chosen entrant \(c\) can be met by taking \(z_c\) sufficiently small. Thus the two opposing directed-cycle conditions are \(	au>0\) and \(2\kappa>0\), so \(f\in F_\kappa\) if and only if \(	au>0\) and \(\kappa>0\). The zero-sign case is infeasible, and the positive-sign threshold is zero but is not attained. Singleton menus and empty comparison graphs reduce to their degenerate probability simplices.
body.justification: The cycle-feasibility regions give an exact design-by-design classification, and the displayed entry table fixes both the strict price sign and the unattained zero threshold that a blanket sign rule misses.
body.gap: Pakes et al. Theorem 2.3(a), PDF p. 20, derives its adjacent-period inequality under Condition 2.2 with both comparator subsets equal in a common choice universe; it does not classify response-table feasibility intervals or terminal inclusion when entry or exit changes the comparison graph.
body.consumer: Designers can screen upper-tail-uninformative cells by finite cycle tests and validate implementations against the explicit entry, common-menu, and degenerate boundary cases.
body.proof_tex:
Assume first that \(M_1=M_2\), and fix \(d'\in A\).  Subtracting the period-specific constants common to all alternatives, define
\[
 g_{1d}=-p_{1d}-\mathbf 1\{h_0\ne d\}\kappa,
 \qquad
 g_{2d}(d')=-p_{2d}-\mathbf 1\{d'\ne d\}\kappa,
 \qquad
 \Delta_d(d')=g_{2d}(d')-g_{1d}.
\]
The displayed premise in the proposition says exactly that
\[
 \Delta_d(d')\ge\Delta_c(d')
 \quad\text{for every }d\in A, c\in M_1\setminus A.
\]
For a fixed shock vector \(z\), suppose the first-period unique maximizer \(d\) lies in \(A\).  For every \(c\notin A\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [g_{2d}(d')+z_d]-[g_{2c}(d')+z_c]
 &=[g_{1d}+z_d-(g_{1c}+z_c)]
   +[\Delta_d(d')-\Delta_c(d')]\\
 &>0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus, using the same \(z\), period-two choice under lag \(d'\) must also lie in \(A\).  Conditional on \(\lambda\), let \(q_A(\lambda)\) be the probability that a one-period draw makes the period-one choice lie in \(A\).  Conditional homogeneity, independence, and the preceding samplewise containment imply, for every \(d'\in A\),
\[
 \Pr(Y_2\in A\mid Y_1=d',\lambda)\ge q_A(\lambda).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr(Y_1\in A,Y_2\in A\mid\lambda)
 &=\sum_{d'\in A}\Pr(Y_1=d'\mid\lambda)
       \Pr(Y_2\in A\mid Y_1=d',\lambda)\\
 &\ge q_A(\lambda)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Integration and the identity
\(\mathbb E[q_A^2]-(\mathbb E q_A)^2
=\mathbb E[(q_A-\mathbb E q_A)^2]\ge0\)
give
\[
 \Pr(Y_1\in A,Y_2\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)
 \ge\Pr(Y_1\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)^2.
\]
If the right marginal is positive, division gives the ratio form; if it is zero, that conditional ratio need not be defined.  When \(A=M_1\), both sides equal one.  With changing menus, the displayed common-menu premise is not well typed for one common inside--outside partition: an entrant or exiting alternative lacks one of the two comparisons used in the equality above.  Hence the samplewise containment argument does not apply directly to the full changing menus.

For any response table \(f\), the strict-cycle lemma and the definition of \(I_f\) give
\[
 f\in F_\kappa\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\kappa\in I_f.
\]
Because \(I_f\) is the intersection of finitely many strict affine inequalities \(A_C+B_C\kappa>0\), it is unbounded above if and only if no inequality supplies a finite upper bound; equivalently, it then contains \((k_f,+\infty)\) for some finite \(k_f\).  By the definition of terminal feasibility, this is equivalent to \(f\in F_\infty\).  Therefore every table feasible at some finite price is terminal-feasible exactly when every \(I_f\) is empty or unbounded above.  Under this response-type condition \(F_\kappa\subseteq F_\infty\) for every \(\kappa\), whence
\[
 \mathcal C_\kappa\subseteq\mathcal C_\infty.
\]
If \(P\) is rationalizable, it belongs to some \(\mathcal C_\kappa\), hence to \(\mathcal C_\infty\); the terminal-frontier theorem then gives \(U(P)=+\infty\).

Finally consider the stated pure-entry response table.  Period-one choice of \(b\) over \(a\) is
\[
 z_a-z_b<p_{1a}-p_{1b}-\kappa.
\]
Period-two choice of \(a\) after lag \(a\), and choice of \(b\) after lag \(b\), respectively require
\[
 p_{2a}-p_{2b}-\kappa<z_a-z_b,
 \qquad
 z_a-z_b<p_{2a}-p_{2b}+\kappa.
\]
The intersection is nonempty exactly when
\[
 (p_{1a}-p_{1b})-(p_{2a}-p_{2b})=\tau>0
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 2\kappa>0.
\]
The entrant \(c\) is never designated as a winner, and all comparisons against it are satisfied simultaneously by choosing \(z_c\) sufficiently small.  Thus \(f\in F_\kappa\) exactly when \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa>0\).  Strictness excludes both the zero-sign case and the threshold \(\kappa=0\).  If a menu is a singleton, or a comparison graph has no edge, the corresponding choice is forced and the compatible body reduces to the appropriate degenerate probability simplex, as the definitions assert.
